quiz.prompt: What experimental signature is taken as evidence for cortical criticality?
quiz.answer: Neuronal avalanches whose sizes follow a power-law distribution, along with long-range correlations.

quiz.prompt: Why might operating near a critical point be computationally advantageous?
quiz.answer: Near criticality a network has maximal susceptibility and dynamic range, jointly maximizing sensitivity, information transmission, and storage — small inputs can produce large, scale-free responses.

atoms.title: Theories of consciousness
atoms.summary: Competing frameworks — global workspace and integrated information chief among them — try to specify what physical processes give rise to subjective experience.

depths.eli5: Why does any of this brain activity feel like something from the inside? Two leading ideas: consciousness is what gets broadcast to the whole brain, or it's how deeply a system's information is woven together.
depths.core: Global Workspace Theory (Baars; Dehaene) holds that information becomes conscious when it is broadcast widely across the brain via a frontoparietal 'workspace,' making it available to many systems; the empirical marker is a late, all-or-none 'ignition' of activity. Integrated Information Theory (Tononi) instead identifies consciousness with integrated information Φ — the degree to which a system's whole specifies more than its parts — and predicts a posterior cortical 'hot zone.' The two make different, testable predictions about which brain events accompany experience.
depths.deep: GWT is a functional/access account (what makes information globally available and reportable); IIT is an intrinsic account starting from phenomenology and deriving physical requirements, yielding the counterintuitive claim that feedforward systems (and some non-brain structures) have low Φ regardless of behavior. Adversarial collaborations have begun testing their predictions head-to-head against neural data. The 'hard problem' — why integration or broadcast should feel like anything — remains unresolved, and measuring Φ in real brains is intractable, keeping this the most contested frontier of the branch.

quiz.prompt: Contrast the core claim of Global Workspace Theory with that of Integrated Information Theory.
quiz.answer: GWT: information is conscious when broadcast widely across a frontoparietal workspace (access/ignition). IIT: consciousness is integrated information Φ — how much a system's whole specifies beyond its parts — centered on a posterior 'hot zone.'

quiz.prompt: Explain to a beginner why these theories don't solve the 'hard problem' of consciousness.
quiz.answer: Both describe which physical processes correlate with or constitute consciousness, but neither explains why those processes should be accompanied by subjective experience at all — the gap between mechanism and 'what it feels like' remains.

atoms.title: Brain–computer interfaces
atoms.summary: Decoding population activity lets the brain control external devices, and stimulation can write information back in.

depths.eli5: By listening to many neurons at once and learning what their pattern means, a computer can let a paralyzed person move a cursor or robotic arm just by intending to. Stimulation can even feed sensation back.
depths.core: A BCI records neural activity (spikes, local field potentials, ECoG, or non-invasive EEG/fMRI), decodes the intended action from population patterns, and drives an effector — cursor, robotic arm, or speech synthesizer. Intracortical arrays in motor/premotor cortex have enabled people with paralysis to control robotic limbs and, recently, to decode attempted speech at high rates. Writing in — microstimulation for artificial touch — closes the loop.
depths.deep: BCIs work because motor intention is encoded in low-dimensional population dynamics that a decoder (often a Kalman filter or recurrent network) can read even from a modest sample of neurons; closed-loop adaptation lets user and decoder co-learn. Key frontiers are stability over years (electrode/tissue interface), bandwidth, fully bidirectional sensory feedback, and the ethics of neural read/write access. BCIs are the most direct test that the population-coding and motor-control principles in this branch are literally correct — they have to be, or the device wouldn't move.

atoms.note: BCIs are an existence proof: if population codes and motor representations were wrong, decoded cursors and limbs wouldn't move — they do.
sources: PMC open-access (intracortical BCI & speech decoding reviews)

quiz.prompt: What are the three core stages of a motor brain–computer interface?
quiz.answer: Record neural activity, decode the intended action from population patterns, and drive an external effector (cursor, robotic arm, or speech output).

quiz.prompt: Why can a decoder reconstruct intended movement from only a modest sample of cortical neurons?
quiz.answer: Movement intention is encoded in low-dimensional population dynamics, so even a limited but representative neuron sample carries enough of the shared signal for a decoder (e.g., Kalman filter) to recover it, especially with closed-loop co-adaptation.

atoms.title: Connectomics & network neuroscience
atoms.summary: Mapping the brain's wiring at micro and macro scales seeks the structural substrate of its computations.

depths.eli5: Scientists are making complete wiring diagrams of brains — every neuron and every connection — to understand how structure produces function, the way a circuit diagram explains a device.
depths.core: Connectomics reconstructs neural wiring diagrams: the full ~302-neuron connectome of C. elegans, the complete adult fruit-fly brain connectome (~140,000 neurons), and dense electron-microscopy reconstructions of cubic-millimeter mammalian cortex. At the macro scale, diffusion MRI and functional connectivity reveal large-scale networks and hubs. The goal is to relate this graph structure to dynamics, computation, and behavior.
depths.deep: Brain graphs show stereotyped organization — small-world topology (high clustering + short paths), a rich club of densely interconnected hubs, and modular communities — that balances integration against wiring cost. But structure underdetermines function: the same connectome supports many dynamical states set by neuromodulation and plasticity, and C. elegans showed that even a complete wiring diagram doesn't immediately yield behavior. Connectomics provides the scaffold on which the rest of this branch's dynamics must be hung.

atoms.note: A complete connectome (C. elegans, fly) is necessary but not sufficient — structure constrains, but neuromodulation and plasticity set the actual dynamics.

quiz.prompt: Name one organism with a complete connectome and one organizational feature seen in brain networks.
quiz.answer: C. elegans (or the adult fruit fly) has a complete connectome; brain networks show small-world topology, hub 'rich clubs,' and modular community structure.

quiz.prompt: Why doesn't having a complete connectome immediately explain behavior?
quiz.answer: Structure underdetermines dynamics: the same wiring supports many functional states depending on neuromodulation, synaptic weights, and plasticity, so the connectome constrains but doesn't fix what the network computes.
